A Spanish trading post and fort founded in 1884 on the Dakhla peninsula on the Atlantic coast of the Sahara, named Villa Cisneros, the start of the colony of Spanish Sahara.

Spain claimed the coast of Rio de Oro at the time of the Berlin Conference, mainly to protect its Canary Islands fishing grounds. For decades its rule hardly reached past a few coastal posts, while Sahrawi nomad tribes moved freely across the desert. Borders with French territory were fixed only in the early 1900s. Today Dakhla is a Moroccan-held city and a centre of fishing and tourism, claimed by the Polisario Front. See also Western Sahara.
